questions.stem: What is the normal range for blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation: Normal blood glucose levels are maintained between approximately 4-8 mmol/L. Levels below this range (hypoglycaemia) or above it (hyperglycaemia) can both be dangerous and must be corrected by hormonal control.

questions.stem: When blood glucose rises after a meal, which hormone is released to lower it?
questions.explanation: When blood glucose rises (e.g. after eating), the beta cells in the pancreas detect this and release insulin. Insulin causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, lowering blood glucose levels.

questions.stem: What does glucagon cause the liver to do?
questions.explanation: Glucagon is released when blood glucose is too low. It causes the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis), which is released into the blood to raise blood glucose levels back to normal.

questions.stem: Blood glucose control is an example of which type of mechanism?
questions.explanation: Blood glucose control is a classic example of negative feedback. When glucose rises, insulin is released to lower it; when glucose falls, glucagon is released to raise it. In both cases, the response counteracts the original change.

questions.stem: Which cells in the pancreas produce insulin?
questions.explanation: Beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas produce insulin. Alpha cells in the same islets produce glucagon. Together, these two hormones work antagonistically to keep blood glucose within the normal range.

options.text: The release of insulin from the pancreas
The breakdown of glycogen to glucose
The production of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources
The conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage

questions.explanation: Glycogenesis is the conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage in the liver and muscles. It is stimulated by insulin when blood glucose levels are high, helping to remove excess glucose from the blood.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous if blood glucose drops too low (hypoglycaemia)?

options.text: The brain cannot function properly, potentially causing unconsciousness
Enzymes in the stomach will stop working
The kidneys will stop filtering blood

questions.explanation: The brain relies almost entirely on glucose for energy. If blood glucose drops too low, brain cells cannot carry out respiration effectively, leading to confusion, dizziness, unconsciousness, and potentially death if not corrected.
